title: Modeling Covariate Transition for Efficient Estimation of Longitudinal Treatment Effects in Randomized Experiments
claim: Across time horizons, adjusted estimators with flexible transition models give lower error and tighter intervals than the empirical baseline while keeping near-nominal coverage.
layout: 3 panels in a row, shared x-axis, one shared legend below
description: A row of three line plots that share the x-axis, 'Time horizon' from 1 to 7. The left panel shows RMSE, the middle panel shows average confidence-interval length, and the right panel shows coverage probability. Five series appear in each panel, each with its own marker and color: OLS x VAR (blue circles), OLS x MLP (orange squares), RF x VAR (green diamonds), RF x MLP (red triangles), and Empirical (purple inverted triangles). RMSE and CI length rise with the horizon. The Empirical baseline is highest, and RF x MLP is lowest. In the coverage panel the lines fluctuate around a dotted line at the nominal 0.95 level. One legend in a rounded box sits below all three panels. The eye goes first to the purple Empirical line sitting above the others.
caption: Dynamic regression-adjusted estimator
abstract: We present a regression-adjustment framework designed for the estimation of longitudinal treatment effects in randomized experiments under static regimes. While regression-adjustment methods are useful for variance reduction in randomized experiments by using pre-treatment covariates, they usually focus only on average effects, from which we cannot obtain valuable insights into when the effects appear and how long they continue. To address this issue, we consider intermediate outcomes and evolving post-treatment covariates over time, and we represent such dynamic trajectories using transition kernels. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic normality and the semiparametric efficiency bound for our estimator, enabling more powerful statistical inference. Simulation studies and empirical analysis using A/B test data from a streaming platform in Japan show the practical advantages of our method.
